subject: physics_2
question_text: Deduce an expression for the force on a current carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field. Derive an expression for the force per unit length between two parallel current carrying conductors?

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1+1+1+2 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are both STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Physics hand-checked: i = nqvA, f = qvB sin θ, F = (nlA)f = B i l sin θ, vector form F = i(l × B); then B₁ = μ₀i₁/2πr, F₂ = i₂lB₁ = μ₀i₁i₂l/2πr and F₁ = i₁lB₂ equal to it, so F/l = μ₀i₁i₂/2πr, attractive for currents in the same direction — all matching the book. The book's printed question reads 'megnetic field' and 'Derive on expression'; corrected here to 'magnetic field' and 'Derive an expression'. ONE DEPARTURE FROM THE BOOK'S FIGURE: the book draws the force F in the plane of the page while also drawing B in that plane. With the current and the field both in the page, F = i(l × B) is perpendicular to the page, so the first figure here shows F as ⊙ out of the page; the algebra is unchanged and the book's drawing is noted in the figure step's why line.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.
insider_note: Two halves, but not four marks each way: the force on a conductor carries 3 and the parallel-wire result 5. A full first half with no second half earns 3 of 8, so budget the time for both.

steps.label: The conductor in the field

elements.text: F is out of the page

steps.margin_note: A wire of length l carrying current i, the uniform field B at an angle θ to the wire, and the force F out of the page.
steps.why: The book draws F as an arrow in the plane of the page, but with both the current and the field drawn in that plane F = i(l × B) must point out of it, so the ⊙ symbol is used here; the formula worked out below is the same either way.
common_mistakes: Measuring θ between the wire and the force. It is the angle between the wire and the field.
Drawing F along the field. F is perpendicular to both the wire and the field.

steps.mark_note: F = B i l sin θ

of the wire is n l A, so the total force is

lines.text: F = (n l A) f = n l A q v B sin θ

F = B i l sin θ

steps.margin_note: Third mark. Multiply the single-charge force by the number of electrons, then bring back i = nqvA so the microscopic terms disappear.
steps.why: Every microscopic quantity — n, q, v, A — collects into the single measured quantity i, which is why the final formula uses only things a student can read off an instrument.
common_mistakes: Multiplying by n alone instead of by n l A.
Leaving n, q and v in the final answer instead of grouping them into i.

steps.label: Two parallel conductors
steps.margin_note: Two long parallel wires a distance r apart carrying currents i₁ and i₂ in the same direction, with the two forces drawn towards each other.
steps.why: Drawing both currents upward fixes one case: the arrows then point towards each other, which is the attraction the algebra will produce.
common_mistakes: Drawing the two forces in the same direction. They are equal and opposite.
Measuring r along a wire. It is the perpendicular separation of the two wires.

steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. The first wire's own field, at the position of the second wire.
steps.why: Neither wire feels its own field, so each force has to be worked out from the field made by the other wire.
common_mistakes: Using both currents in B₁. The field of the first wire depends on i₁ only.
Writing μ₀i₁/4πr. For a long straight wire it is 2πr.

steps.margin_note: Fifth mark. Reuse the first half's result F = Bil sin θ with sin θ = 1, then put B₁ in.
steps.why: The field of a straight wire circles the wire, so at the second wire it is perpendicular to that wire — which is why sin θ = 1 and no angle survives in the answer.
common_mistakes: Keeping sin θ in the answer. Here θ = 90°, so sin θ = 1.
Writing F₂ = i₁lB₁, mixing up which current is in the second wire.

lines.text: F₁ = i₁ l B₂ = (μ₀ / 2π) · i₁ i₂ l / r

lines.text: ∴ F₁ = F₂ = (μ₀ / 2π) · i₁ i₂ l / r

steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. Repeat the step with the wires swapped and show that the two forces come out equal.
steps.why: The two expressions are the same because the product i₁i₂ is symmetric, which is Newton's third law appearing in the algebra.
common_mistakes: Assuming the thicker or higher-current wire feels the bigger force. Both forces are equal.
Giving both forces the same direction.

steps.label: Force per unit length
lines: Dividing by the length l, the force per unit
length between the two conductors is
The two forces are equal in size and
opposite in direction. When the currents run
in the same direction the wires attract each
other, and when they run in opposite
directions the wires repel each other.
This result defines the ampere: one ampere is
the current which, flowing in each of two
long parallel wires 1 m apart in vacuum,
gives a force of 2 × 10⁻⁷ N on each metre of
wire.
steps.margin_note: Last two marks. The boxed formula, the attract-or-repel line, and the definition of the ampere.
steps.why: Dividing by l removes the one quantity that is not fixed by the arrangement, leaving a result that holds for any length of wire — which is why it can be used to define the ampere.
common_mistakes: Leaving l in the final answer. It cancels when the force per unit length is asked for.
Saying parallel currents repel. Currents in the same direction attract.

recall.must_convey: That F/l = μ₀i₁i₂/2πr, attractive for currents in the same direction, and that this defines the ampere.

same direction attract opposite repel
